entries.f2737a2c18e145522ce1bbd177f6b53ac19274b2: <div sID="gen20417" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Mic.3" sID="Mic.3"/> <div eID="gen20417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20418" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20419" type="x-p"/> What the apostle says of another of the prophets is true of this, who was also his contemporary—"Esaias is very bold," <reference osisRef="Rom.10.20">Rom. x. 20</reference>. So, in this chapter, Micah is very bold in reproving and threatening the great men that were the ringleaders in sin; and he gives the reason (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.8">ver. 8</reference>) why he was so bold, because he had commission and instruction from God to say what he said, and was carried out in it by a higher spirit and power than his own. Magistracy and ministry are two great ordinances of God, for good to his church, but these were both corrupted and the intentions of them perverted; and upon those that abused them, and so abused the church with them, the prophet is very severe, and justly so. I. He gives them their lesson severally, reproving and threatening princes (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.1-Mic.3.4">ver. 1-4</reference>) and false flattering prophets, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.5-Mic.3.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. II. He gives them their lesson jointly, putting them together, as acting in conjunction for the ruin of the kingdom, which they should see the ruins of, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.9-Mic.3.12">ver. 9-12</reference>.
entries.ecd71050ef404c1f472973689028f090435b5b21: <div eID="gen20419" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20418" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crimes of the Princes and Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 726.)</title> <div sID="gen20420" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And I said, Hear, I pray you, O heads of Jacob, and ye princes of the house of Israel; <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> not for you to know judgment? <hi type="super">2</hi> Who hate the good, and love the evil; who pluck off their skin from off them, and their flesh from off their bones; <hi type="super">3</hi> Who also eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them; and they break their bones, and chop them in pieces, as for the pot, and as flesh within the caldron. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then shall they cry unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , but he will not hear them: he will even hide his face from them at that time, as they have behaved themselves ill in their doings. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> concerning the prophets that make my people err, that bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace; and he that putteth not into their mouths, they even prepare war against him. <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore night <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> unto you, that ye shall not have a vision; and it shall be dark unto you, that ye shall not divine; and the sun shall go down over the prophets, and the day shall be dark over them. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then shall the seers be ashamed, and the diviners confounded: yea, they shall all cover their lips; for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no answer of God. <div eID="gen20420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20421" type="x-p"/> Princes and prophets, when they faithfully discharge the duty of their office, are to be highly honoured above other men; but when they betray their trust, and act contrary to it, they should hear of their faults as well as others, and shall be made to know that there is a God above them, to whom they are accountable; at his bar the prophet here, in his name, arraigns them. <div eID="gen20421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20422" type="x-p"/> I. Let the princes hear their charge and their doom. The <hi type="italic">heads of Jacob, and</hi> the <hi type="italic">princes of the house of Israel,</hi> are called upon to <hi type="italic">hear</hi> what the prophet has to say to them, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.1">v. 1</reference>. The word of God has reproofs for the greatest of men, which the ministers of that word ought to apply as there is occasion. The prophet here has comfort in the reflection upon it, that, whatever the success was, he had faithfully discharged his trust: <hi type="italic">And I said, Hear, O princes!</hi> He had the testimony of his conscience for him that he had not shrunk from his duty for fear of the face of men. He tells them, <div eID="gen20422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20423" type="x-p"/> 1. What was expected from them: <hi type="italic">Is it not for you to know judgment?</hi> He means to <hi type="italic">do</hi> judgment, for otherwise the knowledge of it is of no avail. "Is it not your business to administer justice impartially, and not to <hi type="italic">know faces</hi>" (as the Hebrew phrase for partiality and respect of persons is), "but to <hi type="italic">know judgment,</hi> and the merits of every cause?" Or it may be taken for granted that the heads and rulers are well acquainted with the rules of justice, whatever others are; for they have those means of knowledge, and have not those excuses for ignorance, which some others have, that are poor and foolish (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.4">Jer. v. 4</reference>); and, if so, their transgression of the laws of justice is the more provoking to God, for they sin against knowledge. "Is it not for you to know judgment? Yes, it is; therefore stand still, and hear your own judgment, and judge if it be not right, whether any thing can be objected against it." <div eID="gen20423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20424" type="x-p"/> 2. How wretchedly they had transgressed the rules of judgment, though they knew what they were. Their principle and disposition are bad: They <hi type="italic">hate the good and love the evil;</hi> they hate good in others, and hate it should have any influence on themselves; they hate to do good, hate to have any good done, and hate those that are good and do good; and they <hi type="italic">love the evil,</hi> delight in mischief. This being their principle, their practice is according to it; they are very cruel and severe towards those that are under their power, and whoever lies at their mercy will find that they have none. They barbarously devour those whom they should protect, and, as unfaithful shepherds, fleece the flock they should feed; nay, instead of feeding it, they feed upon it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.2">Ezek. xxxiv. 2</reference>. It is fit indeed that he who feeds a flock should <hi type="italic">eat of the milk of the flock</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1 Cor. ix. 7</reference>), but that will not content them: They <hi type="italic">eat the flesh of my people.</hi> It is fit that they should be clothed with the wool, but that will not serve: They <hi type="italic">flay the skin from off them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.3">v. 3</reference>. By imposing heavier taxes upon them than they can bear, and exacting them with rigour, by mulcts, and fines, and corporal punishments, for pretended crimes, they ruined the estates and families of their subjects, took away from some their lives, from others their livelihoods, and were to their subjects as beasts of prey, rather than shepherds. "They <hi type="italic">break their bones</hi> to come at the marrow, and <hi type="italic">chop</hi> the flesh <hi type="italic">in pieces as for the pot.</hi>" This intimates that they were, (1.) Very ravenous and greedy for themselves, indulging themselves in luxury and sensuality. (2.) Very barbarous and cruel to those that were under them, not caring whom they beggared, so they could but enrich themselves; such evil is the love of money the root of. <div eID="gen20424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20425" type="x-p"/> 3. How they might expect that God should deal with them, since they had been thus cruel to his subjects. The rule is fixed, Those shall have judgment without mercy that have shown no mercy (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">They shall cry to the Lord, but he will not hear them,</hi> in the day of their distress, as the poor cried to them in the day of their prosperity and they would not hear them." There will come a time when the most proud and scornful sinners will <hi type="italic">cry to the Lord,</hi> and sue for that mercy which they once neither valued nor copied out. But it will then be in vain; God will even hide his face from them at that time, that time when they need his favour, and see themselves undone without it. At another time they would have turned their back upon him; but at that time he will turn his back upon them, <hi type="italic">as they have behaved themselves ill in their doings.</hi> Note, Men cannot expect to do ill and fare well, but may expect to find, as Adoni-bezek did, that done to them which they did to others; for <hi type="italic">he is righteous who takes vengeance. With the froward God will show himself froward,</hi> and he often gives up cruel and unmerciful men into the hands of those who are cruel and unmerciful to them, as they themselves have formerly been to others. This agrees with <reference osisRef="Prov.21.13">Prov. xxi. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he shall cry himself and shall not be heard;</hi> but the merciful have reason to hope that they shall obtain mercy. <div eID="gen20425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20426" type="x-p"/> II. Let the prophets hear their charge too, and their doom; they were such as prophesied falsely, and the princes bore rule by their means. Observe, <div eID="gen20426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20427" type="x-p"/> 1. What was their sin. (1.) They made it their business to flatter and deceive the people: <hi type="italic">They make my people err,</hi> lead them into mistakes, both concerning what they should do and concerning what God would do with them. It is ill with a people when their leaders cause them to err, and those draw them out of the way that should guide them and go before them in it. "They make them to err by crying peace, by telling them that they do well, and that all shall be well with them; whereas they are in the paths of sin, and within a step of ruin. They <hi type="italic">cry peace,</hi> but they <hi type="italic">bite with their teeth,</hi>" which perhaps is meant of their biting their own lips, as we are apt to do when we would suppress something which we are ready to speak. When they cried <hi type="italic">peace</hi> their own hearts gave them the lie, and they were just ready to eat their own words and to contradict themselves, but they bit with their teeth, and kept it in. They were not blind leaders of the blind, for they saw the ditch before them, and yet led their followers into it. (2.) They made it all their aim to glut themselves, and serve their own belly, as the seducers in St. Paul's time (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Rom. xvi. 18</reference>), for <hi type="italic">their god is their belly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Phil. iii. 19</reference>. They <hi type="italic">bite with their teeth, and cry peace;</hi> that is, they will flatter and compliment those that will feed them with good bits, will give them something to eat; but as for those that <hi type="italic">put not into their mouths,</hi> that are not continually cramming them, they look upon them as their enemies; to them they do not <hi type="italic">cry peace,</hi> as they do to those whom they look upon as their benefactors, but they <hi type="italic">even prepare war against them;</hi> against them they denounce the judgments of God, but as they are to them, as the crafty priests of the church of Rome, in some places, make their image either to smile or frown upon the offerer according as his offering is. Justly is it insisted on as a necessary qualification of a minister (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">1 Tim. iii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Titus.1.7">and again Tit. i. 7</reference>) that he be not <hi type="italic">greedy of filthy lucre.</hi> <div eID="gen20427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20428" type="x-p"/> 2. What is the sentence passed upon them for this sin, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.6-Mic.3.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. It is threatened, (1.) That they shall be involved in troubles and miseries with those to whom they had cried peace: <hi type="italic">Night shall be upon them,</hi> a dark cold night of calamity, such as they, in their flattery, led the people to hope would never come. <hi type="italic">It shall be dark unto you,</hi> darker to you than to others; <hi type="italic">the sun shall go down over the prophets,</hi> shall go down at noon; all comfort shall depart from them, and they shall be deprived of all hope of it. The <hi type="italic">day shall be dark over them,</hi> in which they promised themselves light. Nor shall they be surrounded with outward troubles only, but their mind shall be full of confusion, and they shall be brought to their wits' end; their heads shall be clouded, and their own thoughts shall trouble them; and that is trouble enough. They kept others in the dark, and now God will bring them into the dark. (2.) That thereby they shall be silenced, and all their pretensions to prophecy for ever shamed. They never had any true vision; and now, the event disproving their predictions of peace, it shall be made to appear that they never had any, that there never was an answer of God to them, but it was all a sham, and they were cheats and impostors. Their reputation being thus quite sunk, their confidence would of course fail them. And, their spirits being ruffled and confused, their invention would fail them too; and by reason of this darkness, both without and within too, <hi type="italic">they shall not divine,</hi> they shall not have so much as a counterfeit vision to produce, they shall be <hi type="italic">ashamed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">confounded,</hi> and <hi type="italic">cover their lips,</hi> as men that are quite baffled and have nothing to say for themselves. Note, Those who deceive others are but preparing confusion for their own faces.
entries.c8a1d07d0d995f22dfc7e16a3557bbded1f751cc: <div eID="gen20428" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crimes of the Princes and Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 726.)</title> <div sID="gen20429" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and of judgment, and of might, to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin. <hi type="super">9</hi> Hear this, I pray you, ye heads of the house of Jacob, and princes of the house of Israel, that abhor judgment, and pervert all equity. <hi type="super">10</hi> They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity. <hi type="super">11</hi> The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and say, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> among us? none evil can come upon us. <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed <hi type="italic">as</hi> a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest. <div eID="gen20429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20430" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The prophet experiences a divine power going along with him in his work, and he makes a solemn profession and protestation of it, as that which would justify him, and bear him out, in his plain dealing with the princes and rulers. He would not, he durst not, make thus bold with the great men, but that he was carried out to do it by a prophetical impulse and impression. It was not he that said it, but God by him, and he could not but speak the word that God put into his mouth. It comes in likewise by way of opposition to the false prophets, who were full of shame when they lived to see themselves proved liars, and who never had courage to deal faithfully with the people, but flattered them in their sins; they were <hi type="italic">sensual, not having the Spirit,</hi> but truly (says Micah) <hi type="italic">I am full of power by the Spirit of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.8">v. 8</reference>. Having in himself an assurance of the truth of what he said, he said it with assurance. Compare him with those false prophets, and you will say, There is no comparison between them. <hi type="italic">What is the chaff to the wheat?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.28">Jer. xxiii. 28</reference>. What is painted fire to real fire? Observe here, 1. What the qualifications were with which this prophet was endured: He was <hi type="italic">full of power, and of judgment, and of might;</hi> he had an ardent love to God and to the souls of men, a deep concern for his glory and their salvation, and a flaming zeal against sin. He had likewise courage to reprove it and witness against it, not fearing the wrath either of great men or of great multitudes; whatever difficulties or discouragements he met with, they did not deter him nor drive him from his work; <hi type="italic">none of these things moved him.</hi> And all this was guided by judgment and discretion; he was a man of wisdom as well as courage; in all his preaching there was light as well as heat, and a spirit of wisdom as well as of zeal. Thus was this man of God <hi type="italic">thoroughly furnished</hi> for every good word he had to say, and every good work he had to do. Those he preached to could not but perceive him to be full both of <hi type="italic">power</hi> and <hi type="italic">judgment,</hi> for they found both their <hi type="italic">understandings opened</hi> and their <hi type="italic">hearts</hi> made <hi type="italic">to burn within them,</hi> with such evidence and demonstration, and with such power, did the word come from him. 2. Whence he had these qualifications, not from and of himself, but he was <hi type="italic">full of power by the Spirit of the Lord.</hi> Knowing that it was indeed the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord</hi> that was in him, and spoke by him, that it was a divine revelation that he delivered, he spoke it boldly, and as one having authority, <hi type="italic">set his face as a flint,</hi> knowing he should be justified and borne out in what he said, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7-Isa.50.8">Isa. l. 7, 8</reference>. Note, Those who act honestly may act boldly; and those who are sure that they have a commission from God need not be afraid of opposition from men. Nay, he had not only a Spirit of prophecy, which was the ground of his boldness, but the Spirit of sanctification endued him with the boldness and wisdom which were requisite for him. It was not in any strength of his own that he was strong; <hi type="italic">for who is sufficient for these things?</hi> but in <hi type="italic">the Lord, and in the power of his might;</hi> for <hi type="italic">from him</hi> all <hi type="italic">our sufficiency</hi> is. Are we full of power at any time, for that which is good? It is purely by <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the Lord,</hi> for of ourselves we are weak as water; it is the God of Israel that gives strength and power both to his people and to his ministers. 3. What use he made of these qualifications—this judgment and this power; he <hi type="italic">declared to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin.</hi> If transgression be found in Jacob and Israel, they must be told of it, and it is the business of God's prophets to tell them of it, to <hi type="italic">cry aloud</hi> and <hi type="italic">not to spare,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">Isa. lviii. 1</reference>. Those who come to hear the word of God must be willing to be told of their faults, and must not only give their ministers leave to deal plainly and faithfully with them, but take it kindly, and be thankful; but, since few have meekness enough to receive reproof, those have need of a great deal of boldness who are to give reproofs, and must pray for a spirit both of wisdom and might. <div eID="gen20430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20431" type="x-p"/> II. The prophet exerts this power in dealing with the <hi type="italic">heads of the house of Jacob,</hi> both the princes and the prophets, whom he had drawn up a high charge against in the former part of the chapter. He repeats the summons of their attendance and attention (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.9">v. 9</reference>), the same that we had <reference osisRef="Mic.3.1">v. 1</reference>, directing himself to <hi type="italic">the princes of the house of Israel,</hi> yet he means those of <hi type="italic">Judah;</hi> for it appears (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.18-Jer.26.19">Jer. xxvi. 18, 19</reference>, where <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">v. 12</reference> is quoted) that this was spoken in Hezekiah's kingdom; but, the ten tribes being gone into captivity, Judah is all that is now left of Jacob and Israel. The prophet speaks respectfully to them (<hi type="italic">hear, I pray you</hi>) and gives them their titles of <hi type="italic">heads</hi> and <hi type="italic">princes.</hi> Ministers must be faithful to great men in reproving them for their sins, but they must not be rude and uncivil to them. Now observe here, <div eID="gen20431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20432" type="x-p"/> 1. The great wickedness that these heads of the house of Jacob were guilty of, <hi type="italic">princes, priest,</hi> and <hi type="italic">prophets;</hi> in short, they were covetous and prostituted their offices to their love of money. (1.) The <hi type="italic">princes abhorred all judgment;</hi> they would not be governed by any of its laws, either in their own practice or in passing sentence upon appeals made to them; they <hi type="italic">perverted all equity,</hi> and scorned to be under the direction or correction of justice, when it could not be made pliable to their secular interests. When, under pretence of doing right, they did the most palpable wrongs, then they perverted equity, and made it serve a purpose contrary to the intention of the founder of magistracy and fountain of power. It is laid to their charge (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.10">v. 10</reference>) that <hi type="italic">they build up Zion with blood.</hi> "They pretend, in justification of their extortion and oppressions, that they build up Zion and Jerusalem; they add new streets and squares to the holy cities, and adorn them; they establish and advance the public interests both in church and state, and think that therein they do God and Israel good service. But it is <hi type="italic">with blood</hi> and <hi type="italic">with iniquity,</hi> and therefore it cannot prosper; nor will their intentions of good to the city of God justify their contradictions to the law of God." Those mistake who think that a burning zeal for holy church, and the propagating of the faith, will serve to consecrate robberies and murders, massacres and depredations; no, Zion's walls owe those no thanks that build them up with blood and iniquity. The sin of man works not the righteousness of God. "The office of the princes is to judge upon appeals made to them; but <hi type="italic">they judge for reward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">v. 11</reference>); they give judgment on the side of those that give the bribe; the most righteous cause shall not be carried without a fee, and for a fee the most unrighteous cause shall be carried." Miserable is the people's case when the judge's enquiry upon a cause is not, "What is to be done in it?" but, "What is to be got by it?" (2.) The priests' work was to teach the people, and for that the law had provided them a very honourable comfortable maintenance; but that will not content them, they <hi type="italic">teach for hire</hi> over and above, and will be hired to teach anything, as an oracle of God, which they know will please and gain them an interest. (3.) The prophets, it should seem, had honorary fees given them by way of gratuity (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.7-1Sam.9.8">1 Sam. ix. 7, 8</reference>); but these prophets governed themselves in their prophesying by the prospect of temporal advantage and that was the main thing they had in their eye: They <hi type="italic">divine for money.</hi> Their tongues were mercenary; they would either prophesy or let it alone, according as they found it most for their advantage; and a man might have what oracle he would from them if he would but pay them for it. Thus they were fit successors of Balaam, who <hi type="italic">loved the wages of unrighteousness.</hi> Note, Though that which is wicked can never be consecrated by a zeal for the church, yet that which is sacred may be, and often is, desecrated, by the love of the world. When men do that which in itself is good, but do it for filthy lucre, it loses its excellency, and becomes an abomination both to God and man. <div eID="gen20432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20433" type="x-p"/> 2. Their vain presumption and carnal confidence, notwithstanding: They <hi type="italic">lean upon the Lord,</hi> and because they are, in profession, his people, they think there is neither harm nor danger in these their wicked practices. Faith builds upon the Lord, rests in him, and relies upon him, as the soul's foundation; presumption only <hi type="italic">leans upon the Lord</hi> as a prop, makes use of him to serve a turn, while still the world is the foundation that is built upon. They speak with a great deal of confidence, (1.) Of their honour: "<hi type="italic">Is not the Lord among us?</hi> Have we not the tokens of his presence with us, his temple, his ark, his lively oracles?" They are <hi type="italic">haughty because of the holy mountain</hi> and its dignities (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.11">Zeph. iii. 11</reference>), as if their church-privileges would palliate the worst of practices, or as if God's presence with them were intended to make the priests and people rich with the sale of their performances. It was true that the Lord was among them by his ordinances, and this puffed them up with pride; but, if they imagined that he was among them by his favour and love, they were mistaken: but it is a cheat the children of men often put upon themselves to think they have God with them, when they have by their sin provoked him to depart from them. (2.) They are confident of their own safety: <hi type="italic">No evil can come upon us.</hi> Many are rocked asleep; in a fatal security by their church-privileges, as if those would protect them in sin, and shelter them from punishment, which are really, and will be, the greatest aggravations both of their sin and of their punishment. If men's having the Lord among them will not restrain them from doing evil, it can never secure them from suffering evil for so doing; and it is very absurd for sinners to think that their impudence will be their impunity. <div eID="gen20433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20434" type="x-p"/> 3. The doom passed upon them for their real wickedness, notwithstanding their imaginary protection (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore shall Zion for your sake be ploughed as a field.</hi> This is that passage which is quoted as a bold word spoken by Micah (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jer. xxvi. 18</reference>), which yet Hezekiah and his princes took well, though in another reign it might have gone near to cost him his head; nay, they repented and reformed, and so the execution of this threatening was prevented, and did not come in those days. (1.) It is the ruin of holy places that is here foretold, places that had been highly honoured with the tokens of God's presence and the performances of his worship; it is Zion that shall be ploughed as a field, the building burnt to the ground and levelled with it. Some observe that this was literally fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, when the ground on which the city stood was ploughed up in token of its utter desolation, and that no city should be built upon that ground without the emperor's leave. Even <hi type="italic">Jerusalem,</hi> the holy city, shall <hi type="italic">become heaps</hi> of ruins, and the <hi type="italic">mountain of the house,</hi> on which the temple is built, shall be overgrown with briars and thorns, <hi type="italic">as the high places of the forest.</hi> If sacred places be polluted by sin, they must expect to be wasted and ruined by the judgments of God. (2.) It is the wickedness of those who preside in them that brings the ruin: "It is <hi type="italic">for your sake</hi> that <hi type="italic">Zion shall be ploughed as a field;</hi> you pretend to build up Zion, but, doing it by blood and iniquity, you pull it down." Note, The sin of priests and princes is often the ruin of states and churches. <hi type="italic">Delirant reges, plectuntur Achivi</hi>—<hi type="italic">The kings act foolishly and the people suffer for it.</hi>  <chapter eID="Mic.3"/> <div eID="gen20434" type="x-p"/>

entries.65374d49de496885191f8500b220b13347a8eb81: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12744"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mic.3.1-Mic.3.12">Mi 3:1-12</reference>. The Sins of the Princes, Prophets, and Priests: The Consequent Desolation of Zion.</title> <div sID="gen23616" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12744"/><hi type="bold">1. princes--</hi>magistrates or judges.<div eID="gen23616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Is it not for you?--</hi>Is it not your special function (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.4">Jr 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.5">5</reference>)?<div eID="gen23617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>justice. Ye sit in judgment on others; surely then ye ought to know the judgment for injustice which awaits yourselves (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.1">Ro 2:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23618" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ea47d7bf377724aa9c0c198e8faa177ee7a908a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12745"/><div sID="gen23619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12745"/><hi type="bold">2. pluck off their skin ... flesh--</hi>rob their fellow countrymen of all their substance (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Psa 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">Pr 30:14</reference>). <div eID="gen23619" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d8074d1f0cb2783f72e0dcca2fc87975325f26b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12746"/><div sID="gen23620" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12746"/><hi type="bold">3. pot ... flesh within ... caldron--</hi>manifold species of cruel oppressions. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.3">Eze 24:3</reference>, &c., containing, as to the coming punishment, the same figure as is here used of the sin: implying that the sin and punishment exactly correspond. <div eID="gen23620" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b1566b9f96bdd3b6bf74185b3373f5e3ad13cc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12747"/><div sID="gen23621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12747"/><hi type="bold">4. Then--</hi>at the time of judgment, which Micah takes for granted, so certain is it (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.2.3">Mi 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen23621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they cry ... but he will not hear--</hi>just as those oppressed by them had formerly cried, and they would not hear. Their prayer shall be rejected, because it is the mere cry of nature for deliverance from pain, not that of repentance for deliverance from sin.<div eID="gen23622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ill in their doings--</hi>Men cannot expect to do ill and fare well. <div eID="gen23623" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a81e1a7af21b517ff8627c950a2848c8eac0d38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12748"/><div sID="gen23624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12748"/>5. Here he attacks the false prophets, as before he had attacked the "princes."<div eID="gen23624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make my people err--</hi>knowingly mislead My people by not denouncing their sins as incurring judgment.<div eID="gen23625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bite with ... teeth, and cry, Peace--</hi>that is, who, so long as they are supplied with food, promise peace and prosperity in their prophecies.<div eID="gen23626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that putteth not into their mouths, they ... prepare war against him--</hi>Whenever they are not supplied with food, they foretell war and calamity.<div eID="gen23627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23628" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prepare war--</hi>literally, "sanctify war," that is, proclaim it as a holy judgment of God because they are not fed (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.6.4">Jr 6:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Is 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference>). <div eID="gen23628" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fbef435b23bb12ae682f7b5ff2007762d28b289: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12749"/><div sID="gen23629" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12749"/><hi type="bold">6. night ... dark--</hi>Calamities shall press on you so overwhelming as to compel you to cease pretending to divine (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.4">Zec 13:4</reference>). Darkness is often the image of calamity (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.22">Is 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Am 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">8:9</reference>). <div eID="gen23629" type="x-p"/>
entries.b69e802a5f2958cf923f48a5f3885896810c7a6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12750"/><div sID="gen23630" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12750"/><hi type="bold">7. cover their lips--</hi>The Orientals prided themselves on the moustache and beard ("upper lip," Margin). To cover it, therefore, was a token of shame and sorrow (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Le 13:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.22">22</reference>). "They shall be so ashamed of themselves as not to dare to open their mouths or boast of the name of prophet" [Calvin].<div eID="gen23630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there is no answer of God--</hi>They shall no more profess to have responses from God, being struck dumb with calamities (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.6">Mi 3:6</reference>). <div eID="gen23631" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfe672e0a2e91a037bcdfd047a4604b24386f5ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12751"/><div sID="gen23632" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12751"/><hi type="bold">8. I--</hi>in contrast to the false prophets (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.5">Mi 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen23632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full of power--</hi>that which "the Spirit of Jehovah" imparts for the discharge of the prophetical function (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Lu 1:17</reference>; 24:49; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.8">Ac 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen23633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>a sense of justice [Maurer]; as opposed to the false prophets' speaking to please men, not from a regard to truth. Or, "judgment" to discern between graver and lighter offenses, and to denounce punishments accordingly [Grotius].<div eID="gen23634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might--</hi>moral intrepidity in speaking the truth at all costs (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Ti 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen23635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to declare unto Jacob his ... sin--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">Is 58:1</reference>). Not to flatter the sinner as the false prophets do with promises of peace. <div eID="gen23636" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d2f9e83444a3fde8f59af6a99e0c2b9ec54a474: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12752"/><div sID="gen23637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12752"/><hi type="bold">9. Hear--</hi>resumed from <reference osisRef="Mic.3.1">Mi 3:1</reference>. Here begins the leading subject of the prophecy: a demonstration of his assertion that he is "full of power by the Spirit of Jehovah" (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.8">Mi 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen23637" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f6e0de48fc6eb4e3ae353454bd34c1fc78c51cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12753"/><div sID="gen23638" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12753"/><hi type="bold">10. They--</hi>change of person from "ye" (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.9">Mi 3:9</reference>); the third person puts them to a greater distance as estranged from Him. It is, literally, "Whosoever builds," singular.<div eID="gen23638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">build up Zion with blood--</hi>build on it stately mansions with wealth obtained by the condemnation and murder of the innocent (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jr 22:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.27">Eze 22:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.12">Ha 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen23639" type="x-p"/>
entries.27e00c503e46cda53a9e2ce3ed3bf715028b8c8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12754"/><div sID="gen23640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12754"/><hi type="bold">11. heads thereof--</hi>the princes of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen23640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judge for reward--</hi>take bribes as judges (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.3">Mi 7:3</reference>).<div eID="gen23641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">priests teach for hire--</hi>It was their duty to teach the law and to decide controversies gratuitously (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.11">Le 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.17.11">De 17:11</reference>; Mal 2:7; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.6.13">Jr 6:13</reference>; Jude 11).<div eID="gen23642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophets ... divine--</hi>that is, false prophets.<div eID="gen23643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23644" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Is not the Lord among us?--</hi>namely in the temple (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.2">Is 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jr 7:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.8-Jer.7.11">8-11</reference>). <div eID="gen23644" type="x-p"/>
entries.a40ea53d4db8a79758ce33d7be5ae6f40171a037: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12755"/><div sID="gen23645" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12755"/>12. <reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jr 26:18</reference> quotes this verse. The Talmud and Maimonides record that at the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans under Titus, Terentius Rufus, who was left in command of the army, with a ploughshare tore up the foundations of the temple.<div eID="gen23645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mountain of the house--</hi>the height on which the temple stands.<div eID="gen23646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the high places of the forest--</hi>shall become as heights in a forest overrun with wild shrubs and brushwood. <chapter eID="Mic.3"/>

entries.90a17bc24ae4fdcd94289dd07a53ddbc82fed8ec: <div eID="gen34754" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34755" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34756" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34756" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34755" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34757" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the prophet inveighs with great boldness and spirit against the princes and prophets of Judah; and foretells the destruction of Jerusalem as the consequence of their iniquity, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.1-Mic.3.12">Mic 3:1-12</reference>. The last verse was fulfilled to a certain extent by Nebuchadnezzar; but most fully and literally by the Romans under Titus. See Josephus. <div eID="gen34757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34758" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34759" type="x-p"/> Hear - O heads of Jacob - The metaphor of the flock is still carried on. The chiefs of Jacob, and the princes of Israel, instead of taking care of the flocks, defending them, and finding them pasture, oppressed them in various ways. They are like wolves, who tear the skin of the sheep, and the flesh off their bones. This applies to all unjust and oppressive rulers. <div eID="gen34759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34760" type="x-p"/> Suetonius tells us, in his Life of Tiberius, that when the governors of provinces wrote to the emperor, entreating him to increase the tributes, he wrote back: "It is the property of a good shepherd to shear his sheep, not to skin them." Praesidibus onerandas tributo provincias suadentibus rescripsit: Boni Pastoris esse Tondere pecus, non Deglubebe. This is a maxim which many rulers of the earth do not seem to understand.
entries.9cd0713e415bba780ce01257fe9c740358e239fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34761" type="x-p"/> Then shall they cry - When calamity comes upon these oppressors, they shall cry for deliverance: but they shall not be heard; because, in their unjust exactions upon the people, they went on ruthlessly, and would not hear the cry of the oppressed.
entries.d0ab8142e6af5bd6649317b03ba9973be5876393: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34762" type="x-p"/> That bite with their teeth - That eat to the full; that are well provided for, and as long as they are so, prophesy smooth things, and cry, Peace! i.e., Ye shall have nothing but peace and prosperity. Whereas the true prophet, "who putteth not into their mouths," who makes no provision for their evil propensities, "they prepare war against him." קדשו עליו מלחמה kiddeshu alaiv milchamah, "They sanctify a war against him." They call on all to help them to put down a man who is speaking evil of the Lord's people; and predicting the destruction of his temple, and Israel his inheritance.
entries.aacbb5011f3d3a8f3d98e410b99475f4783c3c46: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34763" type="x-p"/> Night shall be unto you - Ye shall have no spiritual light, nor will God give you any revelation of his will. <div eID="gen34763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34764" type="x-p"/> The sun shall go down over the prophets - They prospered for a while, causing the people to err; but they shall also be carried into captivity, and then the sun of their prosperity shall go down for ever, and the very day that gives light and comfort to others, shall be darkness and calamity to them.
entries.388541a5eb148a7d7fe8ce7ec1ba6bc721c23db3: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34765" type="x-p"/> Shall the seers be ashamed - For the false visions of comfort and prosperity which they pretended to see. <div eID="gen34765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34766" type="x-p"/> And the diviners confounded - Who pretended to foretell future prosperity; for they themselves are now thralled in that very captivity which the true prophets foretold, and which the false prophets said should not happen.
entries.e0838ad6bf788841df0f1b0401dc11c94342f7c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34767" type="x-p"/> But - I am full of power - Here is the character of the true prophet. He is filled, all his soul is occupied with power, כח coach, with heavenly energy; by the Spirit of the Lord, the fountain of all truth and might; and of judgment, which enables him to make a proper discernment between the precious and the vile; and of might, גבורה geburah, prevalent power, against which vice shall not be able to prevail, and before which iniquity shall not be able to stand: but all shall fall together, and be confounded.
entries.fd731f555faa094b68126a6dc23bee6d744c09cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34768" type="x-p"/> Hear this - An appeal similar to that in <reference osisRef="Mic.3.1">Mic 3:1</reference>.
entries.4326ff5fb3522a7752873662cbe1aa1135c72723: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34769" type="x-p"/> They build up Zion with blood - They might cry out loudly against that butchery practiced by Pekah, king of Israel, and Pul coadjutor of Rezie, against the Jews. See on <reference osisRef="Mic.2.9">Mic 2:9</reference> (note). But these were by no means clear themselves; for if they strengthened the city, or decorated the temple, it was by the produce of their exactions and oppressions of the people. <div eID="gen34769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34770" type="x-p"/> I do not know a text more applicable than this to slave-dealers; or to any who have made their fortunes by such wrongs as affect the life of man; especially the former, who by the gains of this diabolic traffic have built houses etc.; for, following up the prophet's metaphor, the timbers, etc., are the bones of the hapless Africans; and the mortar, the blood of the defenceless progeny of Ham. What an account must all those who have any hand in or profit from this detestable, degrading, and inhuman traffic, give to Him who will shortly judge the quick and dead!
entries.0868f18ed97545bbe2cd3cebba722be75a0c582e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34771" type="x-p"/> The heads thereof judge for reward - This does not apply to the regular law officers, who have their proper salaries for giving up their whole time and attention to the conscientious discharge of the duties of their office; but to those who take a reward, who take Bribes, for the perversion of justice; who will decide in favor of those from whom they get the greatest reward. <div eID="gen34771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34772" type="x-p"/> The prophets - divine for money - These are evidently the false prophets; for none, professing to be sent by God, used any kind of divination. <div eID="gen34772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34773" type="x-p"/> Yet will they lean upon the Lord - They will prescribe fasts and public thanksgivings, while not one sin is repented of or forsaken, and not one public grievance is redressed. <div eID="gen34773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34774" type="x-p"/> Is not the Lord among us? - Here is his temple, here are his ordinances, and here are his people. Will he leave these? Yes, he will abandon the whole, because all are polluted.
entries.647fae64be1c10932c571aca5f7af76db13f45ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34775" type="x-p"/> Therefore shall Zion - be ploughed as a field - It shall undergo a variety of reverses and sackages, till at last there shall not be one stone left on the top of another, that shall not be pulled down; and then a plough shall be drawn along the site of the walls, to signify an irreparable and endless destruction. Of this ancient custom Horace speaks, Odar. lib. i., Od. 16, ver. 18. <div eID="gen34775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34776" type="x-p"/> Altis urbibus ultimae <div eID="gen34776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34777" type="x-p"/> Stetere causae cur perirent <div eID="gen34777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34778" type="x-p"/> Funditus, imprimeretque muris <div eID="gen34778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34779" type="x-p"/> Hostile aratrum exercitus insolens. "From hence proud cities date their utter falls; <div eID="gen34779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34780" type="x-p"/> When, insolent in ruin, o'er their walls <div eID="gen34780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34781" type="x-p"/> The wrathful soldier drags the hostile plough, <div eID="gen34781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34782" type="x-p"/> That haughty mark of total overthrow." <div eID="gen34782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34783" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen34783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34784" type="x-p"/> Thus did the Romans treat Jerusalem when it was taken by Titus. Turnus Rufus, or as he is called by St. Jerome, Titus Arinius Rufus, or Terentius Rufus, according to Josephus, caused a plough to be drawn over all the courts of the temple to signify that it should never be rebuilt, and the place only serve for agricultural purposes. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.24.2">Mat 24:2</reference>. Thus Jerusalem became heaps, an indiscriminate mass of ruins and rubbish; and the mountain of the house, Mount Moriah, on which the temple stood, became so much neglected after the total destruction of the temple, that it soon resembled the high places of the forest. What is said here may apply also, as before hinted, to the ruin of the temple by Nebuchadnezzar in the last year of the reign of Zedekiah, the last king of the Jews. <div eID="gen34784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34785" type="x-p"/> As the Masoretes, in their division of the Bible, reckon the twelve minor prophets but as one book, they mark this verse (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mic 3:12</reference>) the Middle verse of these prophets.  <chapter eID="Mic.3"/> <div eID="gen34785" type="x-p"/>

entries.d7bd39b597929b1c7afedd72c9da9621dfd40b14: <div eID="gen16547" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">II. Zion’s Deepest Degradation and Highest Exaltation - Micah 3-5</title> <div sID="gen16548" type="x-p"/> The prophet’s second address is of a predominantly Messianic character. The announcement of the utter desolation of Zion on account of the corruption of both the civil rulers and the spiritual leaders of the nation, with which this address opens in Mic 3:1-12, serves to a certain extent simply as a foil for the prophecy which follows in Mic 4:1-13 and Mic 5:1-15 of the salvation with which the remnant of Israel, that has been rescued throughout the judgment, will be blessed in the future. This salvation is depicted first of all in all its fulness (Mic 4:1-7); then in its gradual development, in the re-erection of the former dominion of the daughter of Zion, by her redemption out of Babylon, and her victory over the powers of the world (Mic 4:8-13); and lastly, in its realization by the Ruler proceeding out of Bethlehem, and by the power and blessing of His rule (Mic 5:1-15). <div eID="gen16548" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Sins of the Leaders of the Nation, and Destruction of Jerusalem - Mic 3:1-12</title> <div sID="gen16549" type="x-p"/> The threatening of punishment contained in this chapter is specially directed against the heads and leaders of Israel, and proclaims, in three strophes of four verses each, (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) to the princes, who turn right into wrong and flay the people (Mic 3:1-4), and (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) to the false prophets, who lead the people astray and confirm them in their sin by lying prophecies of peace (Mic 3:5-8), retribution for their wicked conduct; and (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) to all three classes of the divinely-appointed chiefs of the nation - the princes, the priests, and the prophets - the destruction of Jerusalem, and the turning of Zion and the temple mountain into a ploughed field and wooded heights on account of their degeneracy (Mic 3:9-12). <div eID="gen16549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16550" type="x-p"/> Mic 3:1-4 <div eID="gen16550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16551" type="x-p"/> First strophe. - Mic 3:1. <hi type="italic">“And I said, Hear ye, O heads of Jacob, and princes of the house of Israel: Is it not for you to know the right?</hi> Mic 3:2. <hi type="italic">Ye who hate good, and love evil; who draw off their skin from them, and their flesh from their bones.</hi> Mic 3:3. <hi type="italic">And who have eaten the flesh of my people, and stripped off their skin from them; and broken their bones, and cut them in pieces, as if in the pot, and like flesh in the midst of the caldron. </hi> Mic 3:4. <hi type="italic">Then will they cry to Jehovah, and He will not hearken; and let Him hide His face from them at the same time, as they have made their actions evil.” </hi> By the expression “And I said” (<hi type="italic">vâ'ōmar</hi>), the following address is indicated as a continuation of the preceding one. The reproofs of this chapter are also a still further expansion of the woe pronounced in Mic 2:1-2 upon the godless chiefs of the nation. The heads of Jacob are addressed, that is to say, the princes of the tribes and families of Israel, and the <hi type="italic">qetsı̄nı̄m</hi>, lit., deciders (answering to the Arabic <hi type="italic">qâḍy</hi>, a judge) of the house of Israel, i.e., the heads of families and households, upon whom the administration of justice devolved (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10">Isa 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.3">Isa 22:3</reference>). הלוא לכן, is it not your duty and your office to know justice? <hi type="italic">Da‛ath</hi> is practical knowledge, which manifests itself in practice; <hi type="italic">mishpât</hi>, the public administration of justice. Instead of this, they do the opposite. The description of this conduct is appended by participles, in the form of apposition to the heads and princes addressed in Mic 3:1. Hating good and loving evil refer to the disposition, and indicate the radical corruption of these men. רעה, generally misfortune, here evil; hence the Masoretes have altered it into רע; but the very fact that it deviates from the ordinary rule shows that it is the original word. Instead of administering justice to the people, they take off their skin, and tear the flesh from the bones. The suffixes attached to עורם and שׁארם point back to בּית־ישׂראל in Mic 3:1. The words answer to the German expression, “to pull the skin over the ears.” In Mic 3:3 the expression is still stronger; but the address is continued in the form of a simple description, and instead of the participles, אשׁר is used with the finite verb. They not only flay the people, i.e., rob them of all their means of subsistence, but even devour them - treat them like cattle, which men first of all flay, then break their bones, but the flesh into pieces, and boil it in the pot. In this figure, which is carried out into the most minute details, we must not give any special meaning to the particular features, such as that “the skin, and boiling portions, which are cut up and put into the pot, are figures signifying the pledged clothing and coveted fields (Mic 2:2, Mic 2:8).” The prophet paints in very glaring colours, to make an impression upon the ungodly. Therefore, in the time of judgment, God will not hear their crying to Him for help, but will hide His face from them, i.e., withdraw His mercy from them. אז and בּעה ההיא point back to the evil time announced in Mic 2:3. For <hi type="italic">Mic 3:4</hi>, compare Pro 1:28. <hi type="italic">Veyastēr</hi> in <hi type="italic">Mic 3:4</hi> is an optative. The prophet continues the announcement of the punishment in the form of a desire. כּאשׁר, as = according to the way in which, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.18">1Sa 28:18</reference>; Num 27:14, etc., i.e., answering to their evil doings.
entries.303ef91d2b6d98ea20d7002d16644e4a7c85e1a5: Mic 3:5-8 <div eID="gen16551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16552" type="x-p"/> In the second strophe, Micah turns from the godless princes and judges to the prophets who lead the people astray, with whom he contrasts the true prophets and their ways. Mic 3:5. <hi type="italic">Thus saith Jehovah concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth, and preach peace; and whoever should put nothing into their mouths, against him they sanctify war.</hi> Mic 3:6. <hi type="italic">Therefore night to you because of the visions, and darkness to you because of the soothsaying! and the sun will set over the prophets, and the day blacken itself over them.</hi> Mic 3:7. <hi type="italic">And the seers will be ashamed, and the soothsayers blush, and all cover their beard, because (there is) no answer of God.</hi> Mic 3:8. <hi type="italic">But I, I am filled with power, with the Spirit of Jehovah, and with judgment and strength, to show to Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin.” </hi> As the first strophe attaches itself to Mic 2:1-2, so does the second to Mic 2:6 and Mic 2:11, carrying out still further what is there affirmed concerning the false prophets. Micah describes them as people who predict peace and prosperity for a morsel of bread, and thereby lead the people astray, setting before them prosperity and salvation, instead of preaching repentance to them, by charging them with their sins. Thus they became accomplices of the wicked rulers, with whom they are therefore classed in Mic 3:11, together with the wicked priests. המּתעים, <hi type="italic">leading astray </hi>(cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.3.12">Isa 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.15">Isa 9:15</reference>) my people, namely, by failing to charge them with their sins, and preach repentance, as the true prophets do, and predicting prosperity for bread and payment. The words, “who bite with their teeth,” are to be connected closely with the next clause, “and they preach peace,” in the sense of “who preach peace if they can bite with their teeth,” i.e., if they receive something to bite (or eat). This explanation, which has already been expressed by the Chaldee, is necessarily required by the antithesis, “but whoever puts nothing into their mouth,” i.e., gives them nothing to eat, notwithstanding the fact that in other passages <hi type="italic">nâshakh</hi> only signifies to bite, in the sense of to wound, and is the word generally applied to the bite of a snake (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.19">Amo 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.17">Gen 49:17</reference>; Num 21:6, Num 21:8). If, however, we understand the biting with the teeth as a figurative representation of the words of the prophets who always preach prosperity, and of the injury they do to the real welfare of the people (Ros., Casp., and others), the obvious antithesis of the two double clauses of <hi type="italic">Mic 3:5</hi> is totally destroyed. The harsh expression, to “bite with the teeth,” in the sense of “to eat,” is perfectly in harmony with the harsh words of Mic 3:2 and Mic 3:3. <hi type="italic">Qiddēsh milchâmâh</hi>, to sanctify war, i.e., to preach a holy war (cf. <reference osisRef="Joel.3.9">Joe 3:9</reference>), or, in reality, to proclaim the vengeance of God. For this shall night and darkness burst upon them. Night and darkness denote primarily the calamity which would come upon the false prophets (<hi type="italic">unto you</hi>) in connection with the judgment (Mic 2:4). The sun which sets to them is the sun of salvation or prosperity (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">Amo 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.9">Jer 15:9</reference>); and the day which becomes black over them is the day of judgment, which is darkness, and not light (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Amo 5:18</reference>). This calamity is heightened by the fact that they will then stand ashamed, because their own former prophecies are thereby proved to be lies, and fresh, true prophecies fail them, because God gives no answer. “Convicted by the result, they are thus utterly put to shame, because God does not help them out of their trouble by any word of revelation” (Hitzig). <hi type="italic">Bōsh</hi>, to be ashamed, when connected with <hi type="italic">châphēr</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.15.9">Jer 15:9</reference>; Psa 35:26., etc.), signifies to become pale with shame; <hi type="italic">châphēr</hi>, to blush, with <hi type="italic">min causae</hi>, to denote the thing of which a man is ashamed. <hi type="italic">Qōsemı̄m</hi> (diviners) alternates with <hi type="italic">chōzı̄m</hi> (seers), because these false prophets had no visions of God, but only divinations out of their own hearts. <hi type="italic">‛Atâh sâphâm</hi>: to cover the beard, i.e., to cover the face up to the nose, is a sign of mourning (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Lev 13:45</reference>), here of trouble and shame (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>), and is really equivalent to covering the head (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.4">Jer 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.6.12">Est 6:12</reference>). <hi type="italic">Ma‛ănēh</hi>, the construct state of the substantive, but in the sense of the participle; some codd. have indeed מענה. In Mic 3:8 Micah contrasts himself and his own doings with these false prophets, as being filled with power by the Spirit of Jehovah (i.e., through His assistance) and with judgment. <hi type="italic">Mishpât</hi>, governed by מלא, is the divine justice which the prophet has to proclaim, and <hi type="italic">gebhūrâh</hi> strength, manliness, to hold up before the people their sins and the justice of God. In this divine strength he can and must declare their unrighteousness to all ranks of the people, and predict the punishment of God (Mic 3:9-12).
entries.5cbc62e2d8db974fb27cf80dc9adc82e1932d48b: Mic 3:9-11 <div eID="gen16552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16553" type="x-p"/> Third strophe. - Mic 3:9. <hi type="italic">“Hear this, I pray, O he heads of the house of Jacob, and princes of the house of Israel, who abhor right, and bend all that is straight.</hi> Mic 3:10. <hi type="italic">Building Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with wickedness</hi>. Mic 3:11. <hi type="italic">Their heads, they judge for reward; and their priests, they teach for hire; and their prophets, they divine for money, and lean upon Jehovah, saying, Is not Jehovah among us? evil will not come upon us.” </hi> With the words “Hear this, I pray,” the address returns to its starting-point in Mic 3:1, but only to announce to the leaders of the people the threat of punishment for which the way has been prepared by Mic 3:2-7. To this end their God-forgetting conduct is briefly summed up once more in Mic 3:10, Mic 3:11. The summons to hear is really attached to the end of Mic 3:8. They are to hear the sin of Jacob (Mic 3:9-11); but they are also to hear the punishment for their sin, to which the word “this” points. The civil rulers only are addressed in Mic 3:9, - namely, those who were charged with the administration of justice and of the affairs of the state, but who did the very opposite, who abhorred justice, and made the straight crooked, because they passed sentence for bribes (Mic 3:11). They thereby build Zion with blood, etc., i.e., obtain the means of erecting splendid buildings by cruel extortions, and partly also by actual judicial murders, as Ahab (1 Kings 21 compared with Mic 6:16), and after him Jehoiakim, had done (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.17">Jer 22:13-17</reference>). The Chaldeans built with blood in a different sense (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.12">Hab 2:12</reference>). The participle <hi type="italic">bōneh</hi> (building) is also in apposition to <hi type="italic">râ'shē bēth</hi> (heads of the house, etc.), and the singular without the article is to be taken collectively. They do not, however, truly build the city by this, they simply labour for its destruction (Mic 3:12). But before saying this, Micah once more sums up briefly all the sins of the leading ranks. The teaching of the priests for reward refers to the fact that they had to give instruction as to the ritual requirements of the law, and were to do this gratuitously (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.10.11">Lev 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.17.11">Deu 17:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.10">Deu 33:10</reference>), and that in disputed cases the judges were to pronounce sentence accordingly. At the same time, these men (not the prophets merely, but also the priests and the heads of the nation as the administrators of justice) placed their reliance upon Jehovah, upon the assurance that He was in the midst of them enthroned in His temple at Jerusalem, and that He would protect the city and its inhabitants from misfortune, without ever reflecting that Jehovah as the Holy One demands sanctification of life, and exterminates the sinners out of His people.
entries.e36aa35c97476a87dafcb87f990e82033b1a920c: Mic 3:12 <hi type="italic">“Therefore will Zion for your sake be ploughed as a field, and Jerusalem become stone heaps, and the mountain of the house become forest heights.” Lâkhēn</hi> (therefore) applies primarily to Mic 3:11, directing the threat of punishment by בּגללכם to all the sinners mentioned there; but it also points back to Mic 3:9, Mic 3:10, expressing what is there indicated by “this.” <hi type="italic">Zion</hi> is not “the site on which the city stood,” or <hi type="italic">Jerusalem</hi>, “the mass of houses in the city,” as Maurer and Caspari suppose; but Zion is that portion of the city which contained the royal palace, and Jerusalem the rest of the city (cf. Mic 4:8). The mountain of the house, i.e., the temple hill, is also specially mentioned, for the purpose of destroying all false trust in the temple (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jer 7:4</reference>). The predicates are divided rhetorically, and the thought is this: the royal palace, the city, and the temple shall be so utterly destroyed, that of all the houses and palaces only heaps of rubbish will remain, and the ground upon which the city stood will be partly used as a ploughed field, and partly overgrown with bushes (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13-Isa.32.14">Isa 32:13-14</reference>). On <hi type="italic">sâdeh</hi> as an accusative of effect (as a field = becoming a field), see Ewald, §281, <hi type="italic">e</hi>; and for the plural form עיּין, see Ewald, §177, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. <hi type="italic">Habbayith</hi> (the house) is probably chosen intentionally instead of <hi type="italic">bēth Yehōvâh</hi> (the house of Jehovah), because the temple ceased to be the dwelling-place of Jehovah as soon as it was destroyed. Hence in Ezekiel (Eze 10:18., Eze 11:22.) the Schechinah departs before the Babylonians destroy it. With regard to the fulfilment of this threat, see the points discussed at Mic 4:10. Glorification of the House of the Lord, and Restoration of the Dominion of Zion - Mic 4:1-13 <div eID="gen16553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16554" type="x-p"/> Zion will eventually be exalted from the deepest degradation to the highest glory. This fundamental thought of the announcement of salvation contained in Mic 4:1-13 and Mic 5:1-15 is carried out thus far in Mic 4:1-13 : the first section (Mic 4:1-7) depicts the glorification of the temple mountain by the streaming of the heathen nations to it to hear the law of the Lord, and the blessing which Israel and the nations will derive therefrom; and the second section (Mic 4:8-13) describes the restoration of the dominion of Zion from its fallen condition through the redemption of the nation out of Babel, and its victorious conflict with the nations of the world.  <chapter eID="Mic.3"/> <div eID="gen16554" type="x-p"/>

entries.48625a1b2b17861df9fbd822659a505630b1eb5d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mic.3.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mic.3.1" sID="gen87145" type="section"/> <div sID="gen87146" type="x-p"/>The Prophet in this chapter assails and severely reproves the chief men as well as the teachers; for both were given to avarice and cruelty, to plunder, and, in short, to all other vices. And he begins with the magistrates, who exercised authority among the people; and briefly relates the words in which he inveighed against them. We have said elsewhere, that the Prophets did not record all that they had spoken, but only touched shortly on the heads or chief points: and this was done by Micah, that we might know what he did for forty or more years, in which he executed his office. He could have related, no doubt, in half-an-hour, all that exists of his writings: but from this small book, however small it is, we may learn what was the Prophet’s manner of teaching, and on what things he chiefly dwelt. I will now return to his words.<div eID="gen87146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen87147" type="x-p"/>He says that the chief men of the kingdom had been reproved by him. It is probable, that these words were addressed to the Jews; for though at the beginning he includes the Israelites, we yet know that he was given as a teacher to the Jews, and not to the kingdom of Israel. It was as it were accidental, that he sometimes introduces the ten tribes together with the Jews. This address then was made, as I think, to the king as well as to his counselors and other judges, who then ruled over the people of Judah.<div eID="gen87147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen87148" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Hear this, I pray,</hi> he says. Such a preface betokens carelessness in the judges; for why does he demand a hearing from them, except that they had become so torpid in their vices, that they would attend to nothing? Inasmuch then as so brutal a stupor had seized on them, he says, <hi type="italic">Hear now ye chiefs, or heads, of Jacob, and ye rulers</hi> <note n="92"> <div sID="gen87149" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="he">קצינים</foreign>, from <foreign xml:lang="he">קצה</foreign>, to cut off to sever, to separate: they were those who were <hi type="italic">separated </hi>from others, as leaders of an army, rendered in our version, captains, rulers, <reference osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.24">Joshua 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.3">Isaiah 22:3</reference>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen87149" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">of the house of Israel</hi> But why does he still speak of the house of Israel? Because that name was especially known and celebrated, whenever a mention was made of the posterity of Abraham: and the other Prophets, even while speaking of the kingdom of Judah, often make use of this title, “ye who are called by the name of Israel;” and they did this, on account of the dignity of the holy Patriarch; and the meaning of the word itself was no ordinary testimonial of excellency as to his whole race. And this is what is frequently done by Isaiah. But the name of Israel is not put here, as elsewhere, as a title of distinction: on the contrary, the Prophet here amplifies their sin, because they were so corrupt, though they were the chief men among the chosen race, being those whom God had honored with so much dignity, as to set them over his Church and elect people. It was then an ingratitude, not to be endured to abuse that high and sacred authority, which had been conferred on them by God.<div eID="gen87148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen87150" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Does it not belong to you, he says, to know judgment?</hi> Here he intimates that rectitude ought to have a place among the chief men, in a manner more especial than among the common people; for it behaves them to excel others in the knowledge of what is just and right: for though the difference between good and evil be engraven on the hearts of all, yet they, who hold supremacy among the people, and excel in power, are as it were the eyes of the community; as the eyes direct the whole body, so also they, who are placed in any situation of honor, are thus made eminent, that they may show the right way to others. Hence by the word, to <hi type="italic">know,</hi> the Prophet intimates that they wickedly subverted the whole order of nature, for they were blind, while they ought to have been the luminaries of the whole people. <hi type="italic">Is it not for you, he says, to know judgment</hi> and equity? But why was this said, especially to the chief men? Because they, though they of themselves knew what was right, having the law engraven within ought yet as leaders to have possessed superior knowledge, so as to outshine others. It is therefore your duty to know judgment. We hence learn that it is not enough for princes and magistrates to be well disposed and upright; but it is required of them to know judgment and wisdom that they may discern matters above the common people. But if they are not thus endued with the gift of understanding and wisdom let them ask of the Lord. We indeed know, that without the Spirit of God, the acutest men are wholly unfit to rule; nor is it in vain, that the free Spirit of God is set forth, as holding the supreme power in the world; for we are thus reminded, that even they who are endued with the chief gifts are wholly incapable of governing except the Spirit of God be with them. This passage then shows that an upright mind is not a sufficient qualification in princes; they must also excel in wisdom, that they may be, as we have already said, as the eyes are to the body. In this sense it is that Micah now says that it belonged to the leaders of the people to know judgment and justice. <note n="93"> <div sID="gen87151" type="x-p"/> Some, such as <hi type="italic">Marckius,</hi> and also <hi type="italic">Grotius</hi>, take another view of this sentence: Is it not for you, who judge and punish others, to know the judgment of God, which awaits you? But most agree in the view given here. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen87151" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen87150" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mic.3.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen87145" osisID="Mic.3.1" type="section"/>
entries.1674918e839bd3557c67216b549b5a1a158b94dc: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mic.3.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mic.3.2" sID="gen87152" type="section"/> <div sID="gen87153" type="x-p"/>He afterwards subjoins, <hi type="italic">But they hate good, and love evil, and pull off the skin</hi> <note n="94"> <div sID="gen87154" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Their</hi> skin, literally. The antecedent (which is not unusual in Hebrew) is mentioned afterwards: it is the word, people, which follows.<div eID="gen87154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen87155" type="x-p"/>The idea of sheep or flock, to which the people are compared in the last chapter, is still retained here. <hi type="italic">Adam Clarke</hi> quotes from <hi type="italic">Suetonius</hi> a striking answer of Tiberius, the Emperor, to some governors, who solicited him to increase the taxes, — “It is the property of a good shepherd to shear his sheep, not to <hi type="italic">skin</hi> them” — <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Boni pastoris esse tondere pectus, non deglubere</hi></foreign><div eID="gen87155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen87156" type="x-p"/>To “hate good, and to love evil,” in the former sentence, betokens a character dreadful in the extreme; for good here, <foreign xml:lang="he">טוב</foreign> means kindness, benevolence, the doing of good to others; this they <hi type="italic">hated</hi>: and evil, <foreign xml:lang="he">רעה</foreign>, means wrong, mischief, injury, the doing of harm, of wrong, and of injustice to others; and this they <hi type="italic">loved.</hi> How transmuted they were in their spirit into that of very fiends! “They hate to do good, hate to have any good done, and hate those that are good; and they love the evil, delight in mischief, and in those that do mischief.” These words of <hi type="italic">Henry,</hi> no doubt, convey a correct view of the sentence. It might therefore be rendered, “Haters of benevolence, and lovers of mischief.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen87156" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">from my people, the flesh from their bones;</hi> that is, they leave nothing, he says, sound and safe, their rapacity being so furious. The Prophet conveys first a general reproof, — that they not only perverted justice, but were also given to wickedness and hated good. He means then that they were openly wicked and ungodly, and also that they with a fixed purpose carried on war against every thing just and right. We hence learn how great and how abominable was the corruption of the people, when they were still the peculiar possession and heritage of God. Inasmuch then as the state of this ancient people had become so degenerated, let us learn to walk in solicitude and fear, while the Lord governs us by pious magistrates and faithful pastors: for what happened to the Jews might soon happen to us, so that wolves might bear rule over us, as indeed experience has proved even in this our city. The Prophet afterwards adds the kinds of cruelty which prevailed; of which he speaks in hyperbolical terms, though no doubt he sets before our eyes the state of things as it was. He compares the judges to wolves or to lions, or to other savage beasts. He says not that they sought the property of the people, or pillaged their houses; but he says that they devoured their flesh even to the very bones; he says that they pulled off their skin: and this he confirms in the next verse.<div eID="gen87153" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mic.3.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen87152" osisID="Mic.3.2" type="section"/>
entries.e81efcd22140c739d98a33abfc16182010aef7c8:
They devour, he says, the flesh of my people, and their skin they strip off from them, and their bones they break in pieces and make small, as that which into the pot is thrown, and which is in the midst of the caldron
“Under the similitude of butchers the Prophet sets forth their savage cruelty: 1. They take off the skin; 2. They eat the flesh; 3. They break the bones, to pick out the marrow. The insatiable avarice of the princes is described.” — Cocceius.
For when any one throws meat into the pot, he does not take the whole ox, but cuts it into pieces, and having broken it, he then fills with these pieces his pot or his caldron. The Prophet then enhances the cruelty of the princes; they were not content with one kind of oppression, but exercised every species of barbarous cruelty towards the people, and were in every respect like bears, or wolves, or lions, or some other savage beasts, and that they were also like gluttons. We now then perceive the Prophet’s meaning.
Now this passage teaches us what God requires mainly from those in power, — that they abstain from doing injustice: for as they are armed with power, so they ought to be a law to themselves. They assume authority over others; let them then begin with themselves, and restrain themselves from doing evil. For when a private man is disposed to do harm, he is restrained at least by fear of the laws, and dares not to do any thing at his pleasure; but in princes there is a greater boldness; and they are able to do greater injustice: and this is the reason why they ought to observe more forbearance and humanity. Hence levity and paternal kindness especially become princes and those in power. But the Prophet here condemns the princes of his age for what deserved the highest reprehension; and their chief crime was cruelty or inhumanity, inasmuch as they spared not their own subjects.
We now see that the Prophet in no degree flattered the great, though they took great pride in their own dignity. But when he saw that they wickedly and basely abused the power committed to them, he boldly resisted them, and exercised the full boldness of the Spirit. He therefore not only calls them robbers or plunderers of the people; but he says, that they were cruel wild beasts; he says, that they devoured the flesh, tore and pulled it in pieces, and made it small; and he says all this, that he might convey an idea of the various kinds of cruelty which they practiced. Now follow threatenings —
Micah 3:4
